title: Token methods with crypto
idea: Three schema methods mint the project's tokens: two JWTs signed with `jsonwebtoken`, and one short-lived random token made with `node:crypto`.

analogy.text: A bank posts you a code but files only a scrambled copy. When you return the code, it scrambles it again and compares.
analogy.breaks: Only the temporary token works this way. JWTs are signed with a secret instead.

points: `generateAccessToken` signs `_id` and `username` with `ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` and its expiry.
`generateRefreshToken` signs only `_id`, with its own secret and a longer expiry.
`generateTemporaryToken` is no JWT: it uses `crypto.randomBytes(20)` and a `sha256` hash.
Email the `unHashedToken`; save only `hashedToken` and the 20-minute `tokenExpiry`.

steps.caption: `crypto.randomBytes(20)` returns strong random bytes that an attacker cannot predict.
`toString('hex')` turns them into a hex string: `unHashedToken`, the value that goes into the email link.
The email link carries `unHashedToken`. The server never saves it.
`sha256` turns it into `hashedToken`. This one-way scramble goes on the user, with `tokenExpiry`.
When the link comes back, hash the token from the URL again and look for a user holding that `hashedToken`.
A leaked database shows only hashes. Reversing one into a working link is not feasible.

code.title: src/models/user.models.js
code.caption: The three methods, plus lines that call them. Methods need no database connection, so nothing is saved. Step through, then press Run.

walk.text: Demo values for four env settings. The project reads real ones from `.env`.
A small `sha256` helper: hash a string, return 64 hex characters.
`generateAccessToken` signs `_id` and `username` with the access secret and expiry.
`generateRefreshToken` signs only `_id`, with the refresh secret and a longer expiry.
`generateTemporaryToken` returns the raw token, its hash and an expiry 20 minutes ahead.
Build a user in memory and call its methods.
Verify both JWTs, then check the temporary token's lengths, its hash and its expiry.

pitfalls: Email `unHashedToken`; save only `hashedToken`. Swapping them breaks the link or the secrecy.
Use `crypto.randomBytes`, never `Math.random`: its output can be predicted.
Compare `tokenExpiry` with the time when the link returns; the token has no expiry itself.

quiz.why: Hashing the raw token reproduces the saved hash. Hashing the hash gives a different value, so a leaked hash cannot open the link.

takeaway: JWTs are signed; email tokens are random, mailed raw and stored hashed.

starters: Why is sha256 enough for the temporary token but not for passwords?
Why does the refresh token carry only the user id?
Why are there two separate secrets?
